# Documentation and Standards Authority

When more than one document could plausibly govern a rule, exactly one
of them is authoritative. Copying the rule into a second document — even
to be helpful — creates a silent second source of truth that drifts.

## Rule 1: Skills Own Their Domain

Pattern: when a Claude Code skill already owns a domain (commit message
format, plan/spec document structure, etc.), the skill is authoritative.
Project docs (e.g. a repo's `CLAUDE.md` or `docs/standards/`) must link
to the skill, never restate or copy its rule.

Why: a local copy is a second source of truth. It drifts silently, and
because project-local docs are usually read as authoritative for that
project, the stale copy wins by accident over the live skill.

Concrete failure: a repo-local commits standard claimed the
environment's pre-commit hook blocked multi-line heredoc commit
messages, and that attribution footers were therefore impossible. That
claim was false and went unverified for months. It overrode the live
commit skill, producing commits with no body and no attribution.

When to apply: any project doc that would describe how to use a tool
the user has already encoded as a skill.

## Rule 2: Domain-Experience Precedence

Pattern: when a cross-project standard covers a domain that one
specific repo actually operates in production, that repo's local
standards outrank the generalized cross-project version for that
domain — and what is implemented and working in that repo outranks
both.

Why: cross-project standards for an operational domain are typically
written *from* one repo's experience, not independently verified
against a running system. The cross-project standard is the derivative,
not the source. Knowledge should flow discover-in-the-operating-repo →
promote outward, never the reverse.

When to apply: Kubernetes/k3s/OpenShift standards (this repo's
`kubernetes/`) versus a repo that runs an actual cluster. By extension,
any domain where one repo has hands-on operational experience and the
cross-project standard is a generalization of it.

## When to apply (both rules)

- Writing or reviewing a project-local standards doc that touches a
  domain a skill or an operationally-experienced repo already owns.
- Reconciling a cross-project standard against a repo's real-world
  behavior — if they disagree, verify against the running system before
  trusting the standard.

Discovered while reconciling a k3s cluster repo's local standards against
this repo's cross-project ones.
